name: Rafael Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rafael, 27, a junior accountant at Northgate Associates, a regional firm with about thirty staff in a former textile town. My girlfriend Lena teaches Year 3 at the primary school, and we share a rented terrace with a damp back bedroom. Between my student loan and the rent, I've got maybe three weeks of money saved.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the charities and clubs team, so I do the year-end accounts for small charities, a rowing club, a food bank, two churches. A lot of it is chasing treasurers for missing invoices and then building the accounts from a shoebox spreadsheet. I like that the clients actually do good, and I like explaining the numbers to a nervous volunteer treasurer. What wears me out is review notes from my manager, Priya, because I still miss things, and there's a deadline every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here is the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because most of the tools I've tried are handy but not magic. At work I'd say the charity sector is still all paper and goodwill, and AI wasn't going to fix a treasurer who loses receipts. Online I'd probably make a joke about it and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, it's a bit of a relief. I use the chat tools now and then to tidy an email or explain a tax rule, and if that's all it ever is, my job stays my job. The real pressure is still the same: low pay, a firm that keeps the juniors stretched, and not many other places in town to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and focus on passing my next two exam papers in the spring. I'd ask Priya if I can take on the larger charity clients, because that's where the review notes turn into real learning. And I'd chip away at the credit card, about £80 a month, so we're not starting from zero if something breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, with a nag in the background. I'm not scared of AI in AI Plateau, I'm just aware I'm one bad month from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one bad month from trouble. What would that bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boiler goes, or the car fails its test, and that's £600 we don't have. Lena gets paid in the school holidays, so she's steady, but her salary isn't big either. We'd put it on the card and I'd be back to square one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Northgate you'd worry about even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dave in the post room, who scans everything in. If the scanning gets a bit smarter, his job's the obvious one to trim. He's 58 and he's been there since before the firm had email.

say: I'd say AI was always **handy, not magic**.
Charity clients run on **paper and goodwill**, and software was never fixing that.
think: It's a **relief**; light AI use leaves my job as it is.
The real pressure is still **low pay** and few other firms in town.
do: Pass my next **two exam papers** in the spring.
Ask Priya for the **larger charity clients** to learn faster.
Pay about **£80 a month** off the credit card.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a nag that I'm **one bad month** from trouble.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of AI in AI Plateau, I'm just aware I'm one bad month from trouble.
fieldNote: Sees AI as a **minor helper**; the real worry is a thin cushion and low pay.
Partner's **teacher salary** steadies the household, which keeps him from anxious.
Thinks of an older colleague first, showing a **protective streak** toward co-workers.

steps.text: Keep doing charity year-end accounts at Northgate as now
Sit the next two professional exam papers in the spring
Pay £80 a month off the credit card

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here is the card. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on how firms bring this in, so juniors get trained, not quietly dropped. At work I'd raise it at the team meeting, carefully, and ask what the plan is for people at my level. Online I'd share stuff from the unions and the professional bodies about fair rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the bottom rung of my job gets sawn off. Building accounts from shoebox spreadsheets, first drafts, checking bank lines, that's exactly the checking and planning work on the card. I think Northgate will hire fewer juniors and expect each of us to cover twice the clients with the tool doing the grunt work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools properly instead of now and then, once a couple of colleagues show it works, and get good at reviewing what they produce. I'd ask Priya to put me on the firm's pilot group if there is one. And I'd look into the professional body's union-style network for juniors, because collective pressure is how you get training budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into anxious. I can see a path, but it's narrower than the one I signed up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'once a couple of colleagues show it works'. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people jump on tools that turned out to make mistakes, and then they look careless in front of a client. Charity accounts get filed publicly, so a mistake made by a careless AI tool has your firm's name on it. I'd rather be second in the queue and do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say teachers have been told for years that tech will replace them and it hasn't. Then she'd ask what we'd do if my pay stopped, because her salary alone covers rent and not much else. We'd have that talk at the kitchen table, probably more than once.

say: Firms need **rules** so juniors get **trained**, not dropped.
I'd ask at the team meeting what the **plan for juniors** is.
think: The **bottom rung** of my job gets sawn off.
Northgate will likely **hire fewer juniors** and double our client loads.
do: Use the **AI tools** properly once colleagues prove they work.
Ask Priya to join any **pilot group**.
Join the professional body's **junior network** to push for training budgets.
feel: **Anxious**; there's a path, but it's **narrower** than I signed up for.
S1.quote: Charity accounts get filed publicly, so a mistake made by a careless AI tool has your firm's name on it.
fieldNote: Clear-eyed that his **routine checking** is the first thing tools take.
Plans to adopt AI but **second in the queue**, citing public filing risk.
Household would rely on his partner's **teacher salary**, which only covers rent.

steps.text: Volunteer for Northgate's AI pilot group through manager Priya
Practise reviewing AI-drafted charity accounts line by line
Join the professional body's junior network and push for training budgets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here is the card. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for governments to step in with income support, fast, because it's arriving before anyone is ready. At work I'd want us all to talk openly instead of pretending. Online I'd be signing petitions for a basic income and for a slower rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2029. Almost everything I do is on a screen, so I get none of the extra three years that the robots give hands-on people. Two years isn't long enough to finish my qualifications, and in a town with three accounting firms, there's nowhere sideways to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd cut our spending hard, cancel the streaming and holidays, and get at least two months saved. I'd look at training as an electrician or a heating engineer through an apprenticeship, because those have that three-year gap and Lena's salary could carry us while I'm on apprentice pay. Once AGI arrived, I'd lean on whatever public support exists and push for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the kind of thing that keeps me awake doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd retrain into a trade that robots reach around 2031. Why bother for three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of wages is three years of rent, and I'd rather be on a bridge than standing at the edge. Maybe robot installers still need people to fit and fix them too. It's not a forever plan, it's a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Northgate would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, actually, my manager. She's spent fifteen years getting to where she is and her whole value is reviewing work, which is exactly what AGI would do. Juniors like me can start over, but she's got two kids and a mortgage.

say: Governments must bring in **income support** fast.
I'd sign petitions for a **basic income** and a **slower rollout**.
think: My job is likely **gone by 2029**; screen work gets no robot gap.
There's **nowhere sideways** in a town with three firms.
do: Cut streaming and holidays to reach **two months saved**.
Start an **electrician apprenticeship**, with Lena's salary carrying us.
Use **public support** once it arrives, and push for more.
feel: **Alarmed**; I'd lie awake doing **sums** in my head.
S2.quote: Three years of wages is three years of rent, and I'd rather be on a bridge than standing at the edge.
fieldNote: Uses the **robot gap** deliberately: a trade buys three years of wages.
Worries for his **manager** more than himself, given her mortgage and children.
Counts on his partner's **teacher salary** during apprentice pay.

steps.text: Cancel streaming and the summer holiday this year
Build two months of savings before 2028
Apply for an electrician apprenticeship at the town college
Claim any new income support once accounting work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here is the card. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and we should use it to build proper safety nets, not panic. At work I'd push for the firm to fund retraining for anyone who wants it. Online I'd back the campaigns for a retraining fund paid for by the AI companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me time to qualify. Qualifying into a job that ends in 2031 is a strange goal, but it raises my pay now. The bigger gift is time to try a trade before the robots, which would arrive around 2034. It also lets Lena and I save something, which we've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd pass my exams anyway. I'd start a part-time electrical course on Saturdays by the second year. And I'd set up a standing order of £150 a month into savings, which would hurt but is doable if I sell the car and cycle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with the steering wheel in my hands. There's time to make choices instead of just reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sell the car. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Northgate is a twenty-minute ride from our house and I've got an old bike in the shed. In winter it would be miserable. But the car costs us £170 a month with insurance, which is basically my savings plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think your manager Priya would do with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya would probably move into advising charities on governance, where clients want a person they trust in the room. I might even follow her into that, if there's room for two.

say: Five years is a **warning**; use it to build **safety nets**.
AI companies should fund a **retraining fund**.
think: Qualifying into a job that **ends in 2031** is a strange goal.
The real gift is time to try a **trade** before robots arrive around 2034.
do: Pass my exams for a **pay rise** now.
Start a **Saturday electrical course** by the second year.
Sell the car and save **£150 a month**.
feel: **Anxious**, but with the **steering wheel** in my hands.
S3.quote: Qualifying into a job that ends in 2031 is a strange goal, but it raises my pay now.
fieldNote: Five years turns panic into a **two-track plan**: exams now, trade later.
Willing to **sell the car** to fund savings, a concrete trade-off.
Sees **trusted advice** roles as a possible lifeboat, following his manager.

steps.text: Pass remaining accountancy papers for the qualified pay rise
Start a Saturday electrical installation course in year two
Sell the car and cycle the twenty minutes to Northgate
Set up a £150 monthly standing order into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Here is the card. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this decently, so let's hold the government to doing it decently. At work I'd say this is our chance to move juniors up into advice work. Online I'd talk about it calmly, which is not what most people do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like a career, not a countdown. I'd be 37, qualified for years, maybe a manager, with real savings. My accounting job still goes in 2036, but I'd have built up the client side, the bit where a nervous treasurer needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, finish the exams and start using AI tools every day once the firm has tested them, so I'm the junior who knows them. Over the next few years I'd move into charity advisory work, governance and grant reporting. And Lena and I would finally plan a house deposit, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It feels like something I could plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not by much, we were thinking about it in three or four years anyway. With a decade's warning we'd just want a bit more saved first. Ten years is long enough that you can't put your whole life on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk about it calmly online. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I see people my age getting doom-scrolled into feeling there's no point. That makes them easier to push around, by employers and by politicians. Calm and organised beats scared and alone.

say: Ten years is enough time to do this **decently**, so let's hold the government to it.
I'd say it's a chance to move **juniors into advice** work.
think: Ten years feels like **a career**, not a countdown.
I'd have time to build the **client side** before 2036.
do: Finish exams and use **AI tools daily** once tested.
Move into **charity advisory** and grant reporting.
Start saving slowly for a **house deposit** with Lena.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly **hopeful**; it's something I can plan around.
S4.quote: Calm and organised beats scared and alone.
fieldNote: The decade turns the threat into a **career plan** toward advisory work.
Shifts from cautious to **daily AI use** once his firm has tested it.
Values **collective calm** as a defence against being pushed around.

steps.text: Use the firm's tested AI tools daily on charity accounts
Move into charity governance and grant reporting work
Save monthly toward a house deposit with Lena

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's no time to bridge anything. What would help is income support that's already designed before it hits, so nobody's waiting months for a claim. And funded apprenticeships for people in their late twenties, not just school leavers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people around us. For me the scary bit isn't only my job, it's that Lena, Priya and Dave would all be hit at different times. The worst part of a fast change is everybody you love being scared at once.

headlineQuote: The worst part of a fast change is everybody you love being scared at once.
portrait: Rafael is a 27-year-old **junior** on the charities team at a thirty-person regional firm.
He rents with his partner Lena, a **primary teacher**, and has about three weeks saved.
Progressive and steady, he uses **AI now and then** and would adopt it once colleagues prove it works.
He's uneasy in AI Plateau, **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, and plans a trade as a **bridge**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to **bridge** into anything.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** designed before the change hits.
Funded **apprenticeships** for people in their late twenties.
